headlines.title: Power outage near Oakland's Coliseum station suspends BART service
headlines.description: BART service was suspended in some parts of the East Bay on Saturday due to a PG&E power outage, according to authorities. Officials initially said the service was suspended due to a fire near the Coliseum station in Oakland. Later, authorities said BART halted service between its Lake Merritt and Hayward stations due to an “equipment problem on the track.” BART then clarified the service was stopped due to a PG&E power outage near the Coliseum station and said the outage occurred at 4:42 p.m. Just before 9:30 p.m., authorities said the BART service was restored. The service was suspended between the Fruitvale and Bay Fair stations, according to authorities. Officials said alternative bus service via AC Transit was made available.

headlines.title: San Francisco Opera opening night canceled after orchestra announces strike
headlines.description: San Francisco Opera season-opening performance was canceled after orchestra musicians announced they were going on strike on Saturday. The orchestra musicians said their contract expired on July 31 after months of negotiations. “A strike is not something we take lightly, and we are deeply sorry to everyone who planned to spend this evening at the opera,” the San Francisco Opera Orchestra wrote. According to the musicians, management proposed a 26% pay cut and later proposed a 20% cut. The musicians also argued that the Opera is “not a company in trouble”. Sunday’s free Public Opera in the Park performances were also canceled due to the strike. In response to the strike, San Francisco Opera General Director Matthew Shilvock said, “I am very disappointed that the Orchestra has chosen to strike the opening of our 104th season, canceling the opening performance and the beloved Opera in the Park concert, rather than continuing to engage in dialogue at the negotiating table.” The San Francisco Opera gave those with tickets the following options: The ticket’s value may be held on their accounts to purchase tickets for an upcoming performance in the 2026–27 season. The value of tickets may be donated. Request a full refund for the value of your September 12 performance tickets. The Opera said ticketholders can visit its website or call 415-864-3330 to choose the “most appropriate option.”

headlines.title: Fire destroys 2 barns and damages home in Sonoma County
headlines.description: A vegetation fire destroyed two barns and damaged a home Saturday afternoon, according to authorities. The Schell-Vista Fire District said the vegetation fire was spreading to buildings at 1365 Napa Road. Authorities said the fire left a home badly damaged and destroyed two barns, motorcycles and an RV. Authorities said the flames burned one and a half acres. The fire district also said some explosions reported were “undoubtedly” fuel tanks or cans, but that is part of an ongoing investigation.

headlines.title: Judge orders ICE to halt construction of proposed detention facility near Gilroy
headlines.description: On Friday, a federal judge ordered ICE to halt the construction on a planned detention facility after the state and Santa Clara County sued to block it on environmental grounds. In her ruling, the judge said that ICE failed to study potential environmental pollution at the planned detention center and offered no proof that meaningful environmental analysis was conducted before starting construction. Those who oppose the facility are calling this a major victory. “It’s so redeeming because our community deserves better, our community does not want this in Gilroy, and so to hear that the judge aligns with us and knows that it is not the right fit for here or anywhere for that matter, it feels great,” Rebeca Armendariz with the ICE Out Of Gilroy Coalition said. Armendariz has been against the proposed detention facility since day one. Gilroy Sep 8 Gilroy Sep 8 According to court records, if built, the facility on the 24-acre parcel near Gilroy could hold as many as 120 people a day. The state and Santa Clara County joined forces in a legal battle to block construction of the detention center based on environmental concerns, including possible hazardous materials and an inadequate septic system. The judge’s ruling means all construction must now stop. In a statement, Santa Clara County Counsel Tony Lo Presti said, “We’re hopeful the court’s ruling sends a clear message that this is the wrong process and the wrong place for this facility.” Attorney General Rob Bonta said, “The Trump administration tried to rush construction of this facility in secret, ignoring environmental safeguards and shutting out the communities that would bear the consequences.” Last week, before a federal hearing on the center in San Jose, some 200 people spoke out against the proposed facility. State Assemblyman Ash Kalra says the judge’s ruling is a promising sign the center’s future is in jeopardy. “I think that the county and the state are on very strong footing, and so my belief is that there will be a permanent injunction put in place, and we hope it will permanently shut down this project,” Kalra said. NBC Bay Area reached out to ICE for a comment on the judge’s ruling, but have not received a response.

headlines.title: San Francisco firefighters help battle Lucas Fire
headlines.description: More than a dozen San Francisco firefighters were deployed to help battle the Lucas Fire Saturday, according to the fire department. Authorities said 13 firefighters, a battalion chief and four type six wildland engines were deployed to the Lucas Fire. According to Cal Fire, the Lucas Fire has scorched 3,846 acres and is 15% contained. The blaze was reported on Thursday morning and prompted evacuations in Lake and Mendocino counties. The areas MNF-E016, MNF-E018, MNF-E019, UPP-E023, UPP-E025, UPP-E026, UPP-E027 and UPP-E030 in Lake County, along with the MEN-2POT08-B area in Mendocino County are under evacuation orders, according to Cal Fire. In Lake County, the areas MNF-E012, MNF-E013, MNF-E015, MNF-E017, MNF-E021, UPP-E028, UPP-E031, UPP-E032, UPP-E035 and UPP-E038, along with the Mendocino County areas MEN-2POT08-A and MEN-2UKV28 are under evacuation warning, Cal Fire said. An official evacuation shelter staffed by the American Red Cross Northern California Chapter opened at 6 p.m. Friday at Lake County Fairgrounds – Fritch Hall, located at 401 Martin Street in Lakeport, officials said. Evacuees may enter the fairgrounds through the C Street gate or the main gate off Martin Street, and parking is available behind Fritch Hall, the Lake County Sheriff’s Office said.

headlines.title: New rent control measure in Redwood City sparks debate
headlines.description: Volunteers hit the streets in Redwood City on Saturday to get out the vote in favor of a new rent control measure. If passed in November, Measure E would roll some rents back to 2025 rates and add caps on rent increases. It would also strengthen tenant protections and “just cause” relocation assistance in Redwood City. The average one-bedroom apartment in Redwood City is now going for $2,900 a month, and more than $3,700 for two bedrooms. Volunteers said the housing situation will become even more dire if Measure E fails. Diana Lopez said she has been living with five other adults in a two-bedroom apartment for more than 10 years. “Because we couldn’t afford to live by ourselves,” she said. Housing data shows Redwood City’s unhoused population includes as many as 50 to 100 children. District 2 City Council Member Chris Sturken says the rent situation is already critical and without more controls. “Folks in the service sector in Redwood City depend on this measure to be able to continue to live in Redwood City,” Sturken said. Sturken admits rental owners and the city would bear most of the costs, but without it, he says the housing crisis will worsen, especially as new AI jobs bring more workers to the region. But the California Apartment Association says there are already rent controls in place in Redwood City and even more statewide with the California Tenant Protection Act. “The Tenant Protection Act that Governor Newsom signed and heralded as the strongest statewide tenant protection law in the country,” California Apartment Association Local Public Affairs Executive VP Joshua Howard said. The group began its own campaign launch for “No On E” Thursday, and yard signs are already up in Redwood City. Howard says rising costs on things like insurance, maintenance and personnel are adding up, and more rent controls could lead actually worsen the housing crisis by forcing some owners to leave the rental market. “When you limit the ability to recover those costs, it’s only going to make the decision for a housing provider very difficult to decide. ‘Do I stay in business and not make any money, and continue to lose money, because I can’t keep up under this new law, or do I sell my building and leave the rental housing market?’,” he said. Howard says the Bay Area has seen this in the past, when similar laws have passed. But supporters say the danger of doing nothing to further control rent costs in Redwood City could cost a local worker shortage, because more people will have to leave to survive. “The folks in this room, the folks at the grocery store, the nail salon, they may move away,” Sturken said. The “No On E” folks say they will begin their own door knocking campaign as both sides try to sway voters before the November election.

headlines.title: 3.4 magnitude earthquake shakes Contra Costa County
headlines.description: A 3.4 magnitude earthquake struck near Brentwood early Saturday morning, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 12:25 a.m. and was centered 6.9 miles east-northeast of Blackhawk and 7.0 miles southwest of Brentwood , the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. headlines.title: Los Gatos High community remembers and honors Flight 93 heroes
headlines.description: On Friday, Los Gatos High remembered two graduates who were on United Airlines Flight 93, the flight bound for San Francisco that crashed into an open field in Pennsylvania. Todd Beamer and Mark Bingham were among the passengers who came up with a plan to storm the cockpit and overtake the hijackers. A military flyover before the Los Gatos High School football game honored Beamer, Bingham and those who lost their lives on 9/11. Todd Beamer was a baseball player, and Mark Bingham was a star on the rugby pitch. Both were just a class apart. More than a decade after graduation they found themselves on the very same flight that fateful day, United Airlines Flight 93- Newark to SFO. Together they hatched a plan with other passengers to retake the plane from the hijackers. Beamer is credited with the rallying cry “let’s roll” as he and Bingham and the others made the ultimate sacrifice. Congressman Sam Liccardo spoke before the game tonight along with Los Gatos-Saratoga Union High School Superintendent Heath Rocha, who said 9/11 isn’t just part of the nation’s story but also a part of Los Gatos High School’s story. “This broke the heart of every American, on Sept. 11, particularly for folks here at home, it gave us something to hold onto, that we had some connection to those who rose above that moment of horror and terror, to demonstrate the best of America,” Liccardo said. “We want to carry on their story, and the takeaway is service over self. On that day, Todd and Mark knew they were giving their lives up in order to save thousands,” Rocha said. Now, a plaque sits at the front of Los Gatos High as a way for the community to honor Todd Beamer and Mark Bingham and a chance for the next generation to learn about their courage.

headlines.title: San Francisco honors the bravery of flight attendant Betty Ong during 9/11
headlines.description: On Friday, the community in San Francisco’s Chinatown honored Betty Ong, the flight attendant who made the first call reporting the hijacking of American Airlines Flight 11. Twenty-five years later, the community gathered to remember the courage she showed that day with a tribute at the Chinatown Night Market. They played a song honoring Ong. “She’s our hero who stood up and was the first call to report the hijackers,” Rev. Norman Fong, a longtime friend of Ong family, said. Ong grew up in Chinatown and later became a flight attendant. On Sept. 11, she made the first call alerting authorities to the hijacking. She remained on the phone for 23 minutes, calmly relaying what was happening on board before the plane crashed into the North Tower. Because of her call, all other planes got grounded. 23 years later, her courage still resonates with those celebrating her legacy. Ong’s brother Harry joined the tribute, thanking organizers for honoring his sister. “It still hurts you almost die 25 times. Every year yet you yourself want to forget 9/11, don’t ever forget, we just live with it,” Harry Ong told NBC Bay Area’s Jessica Aguirre. Ong’s legacy is a reminder that in a moment of crisis, ordinary people can do extraordinary things.

headlines.title: San Jose police officer fired for misusing Flock camera data, chief says
headlines.description: A San Jose police officer has been fired after being accused of accessing the department’s network of Flock license plate reading cameras for personal use, San Jose police Chief Paul Joseph said Friday. The controversial cameras have been under fire for months with many privacy groups saying the risk of abuse outweighs the benefit of the cameras for crime fighting. “This is a betrayal of the public trust — plain and simple,” Joseph said. “There’s no other way to put it.” The Automated License Plate Readers, or ALPRs, are a big part of police operations, which makes the violation by the police officer significant and an embarrassment to the department. Redwood City Aug 27 Palo Alto Aug 21 Brentwood Aug 17 SJPD said the cameras have been important tools in fighting crime. Police recently used them to track down an exceptionally dangerous armed robbery suspect. Officers managed to track the suspect even after he switched license plates. Critics of the cameras have repeatedly raised red flags, saying they can and have been misused by officers for personal or illegal reasons. San Jose leaders have tried to reassure critics and created safeguards. But on Friday the chief acknowledged the officers in the investigation is accused of accessing Flock camera data on his personal phone to help a family member last spring. “The officer accessed license plate reader data and provided that to a suspect in a domestic violence situation, which enabled that suspect to locate a victim,” Joseph said. “When we learned about this, we immediately placed this officer on administrative leave. We launched a criminal investigation into his conduct. We referred that investigation to the district attorney‘s office and we ultimately terminated that police officer.” Joseph said since learning about the incident, he has made changes to the policy to ensure the data cannot be accessed on a personal device. “I was furious that an officer would betray the public trust in that manner,” Joseph said. “That he would not understand how serious of a violation this is.” Immigrants rights group Services, Immigrant Rights And Education Network, or SIREN, is not satisfied with the fallout and said the cameras amount to mass surveillance and should be turned off. “Mass surveillance is not public safety and these cameras are only creating new threats,” said Kimberly Woo, a SIREN community organizers. “It goes way beyond just one officer and one vendor and one company because overwhelming evidence has shown across the country local agencies and ALPR vendors have grossly mishandled and abused our data.”

headlines.title: Students at Captain Jason Dahl Elementary in San Jose honor Flight 93 victims
headlines.description: September 11 for many is a moment to reflect and honor the victims of one of America’s darkest days. But at a San Jose elementary school bearing the name of one of those victims, Friday’s 9/11 memorial is not only about reflecting, but creating a more hopeful future. None of the current children attending Captain Jason Dahl Elementary was alive during 9/11, but nobody forgets the day on campus. San Francisco Sep 11 Los Gatos Sep 11 9/11 Sep 11 United Flight 93 crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania after passengers charged the hijackers on 9/11. The plane was headed to San Francisco International Airport and it is believed the hijackers intended to crash it into the U.S. Capitol. The pilot on that flight was Capt. Jason M. Dahl “When he was a student, he really dreamed of being a pilot,” Michelle Quilantang said of Dahl. Quilantang is the principal of Captain Jason Dahl Elementary in San Jose’s Seven Trees neighborhood. The campus is where Dahl went to school as a child, when it was known as Hillsdale Elementary. The school today bears Dahl’s name and a tribute to him adorns the main office. Every day at the campus is Capt. Jason M. Dahl day. And on the 25th anniversary of that tragic day, the lesson plan changes for the entire school. In a first grade class, students wrote thank you letters to their heroes. Among the heroes students wrote letters to were firefighters, police officers, teachers, and even Capt. Dahl. Students in a third-grade class used the word “patriot” to write synonyms with each letter — words like “protect” and “thankful.” Meanwhile, fourth graders took a deeper dive into 9/11. “Even though it was 25 years ago, we are still finding ways to make sure the legacy of September 11 and Capt. Dahl continues to live on for our students,” Quilantang said. “And that they ultimately do their best to be positive students in our school community.” Each student also had a second assignment to draw or write a good deed they promised to perform for someone else in memory of Dahl. The American flag at the campus on Friday was also flown at half-staff in memory of Dahl, an American hero whose memory now inspires a new generation to create a better world.

headlines.title: ‘A very devastating impact': Union City community honors Flight 93 victims
headlines.description: On Friday, the community in Union City gathered to honor the brave women and men on United Airlines Flight 93 that fought back against the hijackers during 9/11. There were 40 people on Flight 93, including 33 passengers and seven crew members; all of them fought back against the hijackers and sacrificed their lives to keep Flight 93 from reaching the hijackers’ target on Sept. 11, 2001. The plane ended up crashing into a field near Pennsylvania. “They knew that they were going to be used as a weapon of mass destruction and they chose to die rather than let that happen,” Union City Flight 93 Memorial Founder Michael L. Emerson said. Retired Marine Michael Emerson brought his vision for a memorial to Union City in 2002. Five years later, it opened as the world’s first municipal 9/11 Memorial, a place he hopes will keep the memory of the heroes sacrifice alive for generations to come. Forty granite stones honor the 40 people who lost their lives on Flight 93. The mirrors on each granite stone represent the people who died, and the possibility that any anybody could have been there. “These stones, you have a mirror on the front which reflects how you would’ve acted. The stone side and back are unfinished, and it represents an unfinished life,” he said. Lt. Col Frank Jamerson was in high school at the time of the attacks. His mom’s twin sister Wanda Green was a flight attendant born and raised in Oakland. Green was on Flight 93. “It’s hard, but also the fact that they were the flight that fought back, there is a large sense of pride. It is one of the reasons I’m wearing the uniform today,” he said. “It was a very devastating impact.” 9/11 Sep 11 9/11 Sep 11 Kris Black hasn’t missed a 9/11 ceremony since the memorial opened in 2007. A fellow flight attendant’s son was also on that plane. “It was scary. Actually, as it was happening, I was at the airport and we knew a plane was missing and no one knew it and that’s when we found out it was Flight 93,” he said. “We have to be here every year, especially as crew members, too.” Following the official ceremony, many others also passed by throughout the evening to pay their respects in a more private way, including those who felt a particularly deep connection to the passengers and crew of Flight 93. Some families also passed by to teach their children about 9/11. Carolyn Rapier lives in Union City but says she grew up in New Jersey and frequently takes the same flight that Flight 93 was scheduled to make. “I feel particularly connected to that flight, because it could have easily been me,” she said. Michael Barravechia is from New York and now lives in the Bay Area. He lost coworkers in the 9/11 attacks. Standing at the memorial moved him to tears. “I love New York. This whole memorial for Union City, they did a wonderful job. I’m glad they did this,” he said.
